common_name: Immortality Bearded Iris (Fragrant Reblooming White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Immortality is one of the most dependable reblooming bearded iris cultivars, often flowering again in late summer and fall in addition to its main spring bloom.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely, since covered rhizomes are prone to rot and iris borer damage. Immortality is widely regarded as one of the most reliable rebloomers among bearded iris, producing crisp white, ruffled, lightly fragrant flowers in the main spring flush and then again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season, sometimes flowering a third time in mild winters. Divide overcrowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizomes and replanting vigorous outer fans at the soil surface. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

common_name: Edith Wolford Bearded Iris (Blue-and-Gold Bicolor Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Edith Wolford is a multiple-award-winning bearded iris known for its striking two-toned blue-and-gold blooms.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Edith Wolford is one of the most honored bearded iris cultivars of the late 20th century, winning the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal, and is prized for its striking bicolor blooms combining soft butter-yellow standards (upper petals) with deep violet-blue falls (lower petals), a color combination that stands out strongly in the spring border. The tall, sturdy stems hold up well in wind and rain, and the clump multiplies at a good pace, benefiting from division every three to four years after bloom to keep it vigorous. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

common_name: Caesar's Brother Siberian Iris (Classic Deep Violet-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris rhizomes are planted a couple of inches below the soil surface and tolerate wetter soil and less division over time.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced in the 1930s, Caesar's Brother is one of the longest-lived and most widely planted Siberian iris cultivars, producing tall, elegant, deep violet-blue-purple flowers over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Catherine Woodbury Daylily (Classic Fragrant Lavender-Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Catherine Woodbury is an older, historically important cultivar credited with introducing true pink and lavender tones into modern daylily breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced in 1967, Catherine Woodbury was a groundbreaking cultivar in daylily breeding history, prized for its soft, clear lavender-pink flowers with a chartreuse-green throat and gentle fragrance at a time when most daylilies were shades of orange, yellow, or red. It remains a garden favorite for its refined color and pleasant scent, blooming in a single flush during early-to-mid summer rather than the extended rebloom of more modern reblooming cultivars. Daylilies are otherwise easygoing, thriving in average soil with routine watering, and clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to control size and maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Ruby Spider Daylily (Giant Red Late-Season Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ruby Spider produces some of the largest flowers of any daylily cultivar, so give plants ample room and stake tall scapes in windy sites if needed.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ruby Spider is celebrated among daylily growers for its enormous, nine-inch, deep ruby-red flowers with a bright yellow-green throat, among the largest blooms of any widely grown daylily cultivar, held on tall, well-branched scapes in mid-to-late summer. The dramatic flower size and rich color make it a strong focal point in a mixed border even though it flowers for a shorter overall season than modern reblooming types. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread.
